claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
The limited plasticity of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is associated with its Mo content.
Part of the Mo should be replaced by Nb while the Zr, Ti, and Hf fractions remain unchanged.
Replacing Mo with Nb will lower the alloy's overall electronegativity difference.
The lower electronegativity difference will moderate or relieve excessive lattice distortion.
Moderated lattice distortion will facilitate dislocation mobility.
Replacing some Mo with Nb will improve room-temperature compressive ductility.
The Mo-reduced, Nb-enriched alloy will retain approximately 1719 MPa compressive yield strength.
Refractory-element solid-solution strengthening will be preserved after partial Mo-to-Nb substitution.
The proposed benefit requires the modified alloy to remain a single-phase disordered BCC solid solution without brittle secondary phases.
Excessive Nb addition could reduce strength by perturbing the balance of atomic size and bonding.
Excessive Nb addition could lead to secondary-phase precipitation.
In the refractory alloys discussed by the cited study, adding Mo increased room-temperature yield strength from 929 MPa to 1512 MPa and reduced fracture strain from greater than 50% to 12%.
The optimal Mo-to-Nb substitution ratio is not established.
The strength-ductility trade-off may depend on processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls for reducing Mo below its equiatomic level and increasing Nb, but the example Mo:Nb ratios of 100:0, 80:20, and 60:40 are not anchored to the equiatomic starting ratio of 50:50 within the Mo-Nb fraction. If interpreted literally at fixed Mo+Nb content, all three examples contain less Nb and more Mo than the equiatomic baseline.
